author: Epiphanius of Salamis
occasion: Epiphanius writes to John of Jerusalem to explain and defend his action of tearing a curtain with a painted human image in a church at Anautha, and to send what he has obtained as a replacement.
argument: Epiphanius urges John not to be carried away by pride of office but to heed Scripture's warning against grumbling. He prays that God will crush Satan under the feet of Christians and prevent the bond of Christ's unfeigned love, peace, right faith, and truth from being torn away from them. He then recounts that while traveling to the holy place of Bethel to meet with John, he entered a church at the village of Anautha, found a curtain painted with a human image said to be Christ or a saint, tore it as an abomination in church, and advised using it to wrap a poor dead person. He notes that some grumbled, saying he should have replaced the curtain from his own resources before tearing it, though he had promised to send another. He now sends what he found, having expected to send something from Cyprus, and asks John to order the local presbyter to receive it and to prevent such things from being hung in churches.

scripture: The source quotes 1 Corinthians 10:10 directly without naming Paul, with an allusion to 10:9. Modern citation should be 1 Corinthians 10:10, with possible allusion to 10:9.
uncertain: The exact date of the letter is not stated in the source.
The identity of the image on the curtain is uncertain; Epiphanius himself says he does not remember whether it was said to be Christ or one of the saints.
The location 'Anautha' is known only from this letter and its exact identification is uncertain.
Whether the item Epiphanius sends is specifically a curtain or some other replacement is not explicitly stated; he says only 'what I found I have sent.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: to explain and defend his action of tearing a curtain with a painted human image in a church at Anautha
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ποιήσει μεθ' ἡμῶν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φιλανθρωπίαν εἰς τὸ συντριβῆναι τὸν σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ἡμῶν τῶν Χριστιανῶν καὶ ἀποδιωχθῆναι πᾶσαν πρόφασιν πονηρὰν εἰς τὸ μὴ σχισθῆναι τὸν σύνδεσμον ἐξ ἡμῶν τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἀνυποκρίτου ἀγάπης καὶ εἰρήνης καὶ ὀρθῆς πίστεως καὶ ἀληθείας
_unresolved_facts.fix: Epiphanius writes to John of Jerusalem primarily to preserve unity and prevent schism; the letter explains his tearing of a curtain with a painted human image at Anautha and sends a replacement, but the overarching purpose is to counter grumbling and maintain the bond of Christ's love, peace, right faith, and truth.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He prays that God will crush Satan under the feet of Christians
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ποιήσει μεθ' ἡμῶν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φιλανθρωπίαν εἰς τὸ συντριβῆναι τὸν σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ἡμῶν τῶν Χριστιανῶν
_unresolved_facts.fix: He prays that God will crush Satan under the feet of us Christians / under our feet as Christians (ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ἡμῶν τῶν Χριστιανῶν — 'our feet, us Christians' or 'the feet of us Christians', not 'the feet of Christians' as a general third-person category distinct from the speaker)

_unresolved_facts.claim: He notes that some grumbled, saying he should have replaced the curtain from his own resources before tearing it, though he had promised to send another
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καίτοιγε ἐμοῦ ὑποσχομένου ὅτι ἀντ' αὐτοῦ ἀποστελῶ ἕτερον, ἐβράδυνα δὲ τοῦ ἀποστεῖλαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: He notes that some grumbled, saying he should have replaced the curtain from his own resources before tearing it; and although he had promised to send another, he delayed in sending it (the grumbling preceded or accompanied the promise, and the delay is admitted as a failing, not merely noted as a circumstance)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἔδει ἡμᾶς ἀγαπητὲ μὴ τῇ οἰήσει τῶν κλήρων φέρεσθαι, ἀλλὰ ... 282 ... φησὶ γὰρ ἡ θεία γραφή· (Paul. ad. Cor. 10, 10) μηδὲ γογγύζετε καθάπερ τινὲς ἐγόγγυσαν καὶ ἀπώλοντο ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀλοθρευτοῦ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Epiphanius greets John and urges that they not be carried away by pride of office (τῇ οἰήσει τῶν κλήρων), citing Scripture's warning against grumbling — the exhortation uses first-person plural ('us'), not directed solely at John
